newsitem.title: POLAND: Warsaw meeting proposes steps to fight car crime.
newsitem.headline: Warsaw meeting proposes steps to fight car crime.

text.p: An international conference in Warsaw on car theft, itself a sign countries are taking the cross-border problem seriously, on Tuesday proposed a wide package of measures to fight the problem.

The recommendations call for countries to set up databases on stolen vehicles and link them through a computer system being built up by Interpol in Lyon, France, so that police in any country will be able to check on any suspect vehicle.

The conference, grouping law enforcers, insurers and car makers from 30 countries, also called for greater international cooperation, better training of officials and for car makers to improve anti-theft technology and identification systems for vehicles and parts.

"What we have designed here, in terms of catching car thieves...is a better, effective mousetrap," U.S. State Department delegate Jonathan Winer told reporters after the two-day United Nations-sponsored meeting.
"But if one person puts the trap in his basement and his neighbours don't, the mice come back every day," said Winer, Deputy Assistant Secretary at the Bureau of Narcotics and Law Enforcement.
"What we are trying to do through the U.N. is to get every nation to simultaneously put these kinds of procedures in place, and I think we will get there," Winer said.
The recommendations are to be pursued at a meeting in Russia early next year.
They urge countries to adopt a standard international treaty for the return of vehicles stolen in another country, amend laws to make this easier and introduce common registration procedures.
Car theft is now a multi-billion-dollar business, but Winer and other speakers said that even four or five years ago it was not taken seriously in many countries.

The scale of the problem, the involvement of slick, sinister organised crime groups and booming car theft in states which were previously either transit routes or recipients of smuggled stolen vehicles has made them change their minds.
Conference host Poland, a transit country for gangs whisking cars stolen in western Europe eastwards to former Soviet states, has itself suffered soaring vehicle theft.

Interpol figures show that in 1995, 50,684 cars were stolen in Poland, a 20.6 percent rise over the previous year, while thefts in Germany fell 8.8 percent to 129,652 and several other Western European states also saw declines.
This year, the wife of Poland's interior minister and the top presidential security adviser were among the victims.
Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, reflecting Poland's strong concern, promised new legislation and more effective police action in a speech opening the gathering.

Global figures are unavailable, but in the United States $6 billion to $7 billion of cars are taken a year, a third of which leave the country, while Europe's annual toll is 1.5 to two million vehicles a year, half of which are not recovered.
Cars stolen in Los Angeles wind up in China, Saudi Arabia and Vietnam, sometimes hidden in containers.
A U.S. insurance journal, quoted by a U.N. information paper, suggests that if car theft were a legitimate business it would rank fifth among the Fortune 500 companies.
German police expert Peter Koehler told the conference that counteractive measures had cut car thefts in his country since 1994 and the trend continued in the first half of 1996.

But he said criminals were adopting new methods, including fraud against rental firms or insurers. Many owners were selling their cars to crooks, reporting them as stolen, and collecting from insurance companies.
"We estimate that in about 30 to 50 percent of all cases, the owner of the vehicle is involved, although this is not yet supported by statistical evidence," Koehler said.
